archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense in decline)
archetype.definition: Denver is a .500-caliber team that still gets priced on last year's 14-3 reputation, with good pass protection and an average offense paired with a defense that has slipped from elite to below average.

report.headline: The defense that carried two seasons is leaking, and the corners are hurt
report.take:
For two years Denver won with defense. The unit ranked 1st in EPA allowed in 2024 and 8th in 2025, and last year's 14-3 was padded by a league-best 0.846 win rate in one-score games and nearly three wins over expectation. This year the luck has evened out, with winsOverExpected at 0.07, but the defense has not held up. It is 23rd in EPA allowed, and the 2-2 record sits on a 74-94 point differential, 20th in net EPA. Bo Nix and the offense rank 18th, roughly where they have been in recent seasons. The difference is that the defense no longer covers for them.

The defensive problem is specific: the run fit and the tackling. Denver is last in rush EPA allowed and last in missed-tackle rate, and it allows explosive runs at the 26th-ranked rate. Kansas City ran for 220 yards in the opener, and San Francisco ran for 140 in Week 4. The pass defense is respectable at 12th, and it is very good deep (7th in deep EPA allowed). It gets beaten underneath, ranking 26th on short throws, which fits a unit that misses tackles after the catch. Third downs are also a problem: opponents convert 47.5%, 28th. The red zone, at 7th, has kept the scoring from looking worse than it is. That bend-don't-break profile is fragile.

Some context helps the defense. The four offenses it has faced rank 5th, 7th, 15th and 1st in EPA today, a hard opening stretch. The offense has also steadied after a disastrous opener at Kansas City (-14.4 pass EPA, four sacks). Since then Nix has posted positive pass EPA in two of three games, and the line has allowed one sack over those three weeks. Pass protection is the most reliable part of this team: 4th in sack rate and 2nd in hit rate allowed. The run blocking is weaker, 26th in yards before contact, so the 3.53 yards per carry is mostly a line issue rather than a back issue.

The near-term problem is that the strongest part of the defense, the secondary, is the part that just got hurt. Pat Surtain II is doubtful and expected to miss about two weeks. Riley Moss, who plays 88% of snaps, is questionable with a rib injury. Pat Bryant is out for a few weeks, which thins a receiving group that already runs through Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton. This looks like a team headed for nine-ish wins unless the run defense gets fixed.

strengths.title: Pass protection keeps Nix clean
strengths.body: Denver ranks 4th in sack rate allowed and 2nd in QB hit rate allowed. It has given up just one sack since the Week 1 mess in Kansas City. A 2.95-second average time to throw shows the line is holding up on longer-developing plays, not just on quick throws. This is structural and should hold.

strengths.title: Nothing gets over the top
strengths.body: The secondary ranks 7th in deep EPA allowed, and the defense is 12th against the pass overall. That is the remaining piece of the 2024-25 unit. It depends on Surtain and Moss, though, so expect it to slip while they are out.

strengths.title: Red zone and short yardage
strengths.body: Denver converts 88.9% of short-yardage runs, 3rd in the league. On defense it allows touchdowns on only half of red-zone trips, 7th. These are the small edges that turned two one-score games into wins. They are also the kind of edges that tend to drift toward average.

concerns.title: Worst run defense in football
concerns.body: Denver is last in rush EPA allowed and last in missed-tackle rate, so this is a fundamentals problem rather than bad luck. The defense has also slid from 1st in 2024 to 23rd now. Run-first opponents will keep leaning on it until the tackling improves.

concerns.title: Short passing and third downs
concerns.body: Opponents complete short throws and break tackles: Denver is 26th in short-pass EPA allowed and 28th on third down. That keeps drives alive and helps explain why Denver ranks 27th in time of possession. The Rams threw for 390 yards in Week 3.

concerns.title: Secondary injuries hit the strength
concerns.body: Surtain is doubtful with an ankle injury and expected to miss about two weeks. Moss, a 4-game starter at 88% of snaps, is questionable with a rib injury. Losing both would expose the one defensive area that has held up.

trend.note: The offense recovered from a -14.4 pass-EPA opener and has been roughly average since. The defense went the other way: two sacks and one takeaway in the opener, four sacks and two takeaways against the Rams, then zero of each at San Francisco.

nextGame.headline: A broken Chargers line is the cure for Denver's pass rush
nextGame.body:
Los Angeles is 0-4 and ranks 31st in offensive EPA. The cause is mostly up front: 26th in sack rate allowed and last in QB hit rate allowed, with Rashawn Slater now out 4-6 weeks and Joe Alt, Trevor Penning and Kayode Awosika all hurt. Denver is 6th in hit rate, so this is the week its pass rush should finish plays. The Chargers run more than expected (-9 pass rate over expected) and rank 11th in run success. That aims straight at Denver's 32nd-ranked run defense, so the game likely turns on whether Denver can tackle. On the other side, the Chargers defense is real: 11th in EPA, 2nd in takeaways, 10th in pressure rate. Its weak spot is deep passing, 20th in deep EPA allowed, and Denver's protection should give Nix time to attack it.

The injuries matter on both sides. Denver likely plays without Surtain and possibly Moss, which helps Herbert if he has time to throw, though his line suggests he won't. Ladd McConkey is questionable and Derwin James is out for LA. The 0-4 record also overstates the Chargers' decline: they are -2.04 wins under expectation and lose 4.33 EPA per game on special teams. Both of those are noisy and tend to correct.

keyMatchups.title: Denver rush vs. LA's patchwork line
keyMatchups.body: Denver's 6th-ranked hit rate meets a Chargers offense that allows hits more often than anyone, and that was before Slater went down. Denver's sack rate is only 20th, so the question is whether pressure turns into sacks this week.

keyMatchups.title: LA's run game vs. bad tackling
keyMatchups.body: The Chargers lean run-heavy and rank 11th in run success, while Denver ranks last in run EPA allowed. If LA can stay on schedule on the ground, it can shorten the game and keep its line out of obvious passing downs.

keyMatchups.title: Nix deep vs. a ball-hawking defense
keyMatchups.body: LA gives up deep plays (20th in deep EPA allowed) but takes the ball away, ranking 2nd with eight takeaways. Clean pockets should let Nix take his shots. Ball security decides whether those shots pay off or turn the game.

nextGame.watch: Watch Denver's early-down run defense against a Chargers team trying to stay ahead of the chains to protect a depleted line.

restOfSeason.body:
Last year's close-game magic is gone, and this team plays like its efficiency: around .500, with an offense in the high teens to low 20s in points and a defense that no longer rescues it. The pass protection and the deep-ball defense should hold up. The red-zone and short-yardage edges will probably drift toward average, and the run defense will keep getting tested until the tackling improves.

The schedule splits evenly. It includes soft spots (Miami twice-winless at 0-4 with bottom-five units, Arizona's 27th-ranked defense, Buffalo's 29th-ranked defense, the Chargers twice) and a hard core of Seattle, Kansas City and Las Vegas twice, all with top-three or top-ten defenses. With KC 4-0 and LV 3-1, the division looks out of reach, and a wild-card spot is the realistic ceiling.
swingFactors: Whether the tackling and run fits improve
How long Surtain and Moss are out
Nix sustaining his post-Week 1 passing level

bets.reason: Denver scores 18.5 per game (26th) and LA scores 16.8 (29th). The Chargers want to run the ball and shorten the game, and three of Denver's four games have gone under. Denver would need to beat its season scoring average to reach its implied ~23 points against a top-11 defense.

The line prices Denver like last year's team, but this year it is 20th in net EPA with a -5 point differential. Denver is likely missing both starting corners and laying more than a field goal on the road. LA's 0-4 is inflated by -2.04 wins under expectation and special-teams losses that tend to regress, and its defense ranks 11th.

confidence.note: Four games against a hard slate of offenses, plus significant secondary injuries, but the defensive decline shows up across many metrics.
